A CIO's checklist for legacy modernisation

ModernisationBy the OneClicq team9 November 20267 min read

Most organisations run at least one system that everyone depends on and nobody wants to touch. Replacing it in one big project is tempting, and usually the riskiest option. A staged approach is slower to describe and faster to deliver.

Stage 1: Understand what you have

  • List every function the system performs, including reports, exports and month-end jobs that only run occasionally.
  • Map integrations: which systems send data in, which take data out, and how (files, APIs, shared databases).
  • Find the real pain: speed, cost, security risk, missing features, or a shrinking pool of people who can maintain it.
  • Check data quality early. Years of duplicate and inconsistent records will follow you into any new system.
  • Identify the experts who understand the old system, and secure their time before you start.

Stage 2: Decide the approach

There is no single right answer. For each part of the system, choose one:

  • Keep and wrap: leave the core in place and put modern APIs around it so new tools can use its data.
  • Re-platform: move it to supported infrastructure or the cloud with minimal change.
  • Rebuild in stages: replace one module at a time with new software.
  • Replace with a product: adopt an off-the-shelf ERP, CRM or SaaS tool where your process is standard.

Stage 3: Sequence for early wins and low risk

The most reliable pattern is to build new modules alongside the old system and move functions across one by one, often called the "strangler" approach. Start with an area that is valuable, fairly self-contained and not the riskiest, such as reporting, a customer portal or a single department's workflow. Each completed step reduces what the old system does until it can be switched off.

Stage 4: Protect the business during the change

  • Keep the old and new systems in sync while both are in use, and agree which one is the source of truth for each type of data.
  • Migrate data in rehearsals first and compare totals, balances and record counts.
  • Run old and new side by side for a period on critical processes such as billing and payroll.
  • Have a written rollback plan for every release.

Stage 5: Bring people with you

Modernisation fails as often from adoption as from technology. Involve the people who use the system daily in design decisions, train them before go-live, and give them a clear way to report problems in the first weeks.

Stage 6: Measure and decommission

Define success before you start: faster processing, fewer errors, lower running cost or reduced risk. Track it after each stage. Then actually switch off what you have replaced, including licences, servers and support contracts, so the savings are real.

The one-page checklist

  1. Inventory of functions, integrations and data
  2. Named business owner and subject-matter experts
  3. Approach chosen per module, with reasons
  4. First module selected for value and low risk
  5. Data migration rehearsed and reconciled
  6. Parallel run and rollback plan for critical processes
  7. Training and support plan for users
  8. Success measures and a decommissioning date
